title: The Relative Instability of Model Comparison with Cross-validation
claim: Inference calibration holds for a relatively stable procedure but severely breaks for a relatively unstable comparison of two otherwise stable procedures.
layout: single calibration plot, stable diagonal versus unstable curve below it, legend top-left
description: A single line plot with Target Coverage on the x-axis (0 to 1) and Actual Coverage on the y-axis (0 to 1). A solid blue line labeled 'Relatively stable model' runs almost exactly along the diagonal from (0,0) to (1,1), so actual coverage matches the target. A dashed orange line labeled 'Relatively unstable model comparison' starts at the same origin but bows well below the diagonal. It reaches about 0.3 at a target of 0.6 and about 0.5 at a target of 0.85. It then shoots up to 1.0 at a target of 1.0. The legend sits in the upper left. The gap between the two curves is the main visual point, and the eye goes first to the diagonal and then to the sagging orange curve. The plot uses default matplotlib styling with no annotations.
caption: The cross-validation central limit theorem [ref] yields accurate coverage for the relatively stable Lasso algorithm but severely undercovers for the relatively unstable comparison of two Lasso fits. See [ref] for full experiment details.
abstract: Cross-validation (CV) is known to provide asymptotically exact tests and confidence intervals for model improvement but only when the model comparison is relatively stable. Surprisingly, we prove that even simple, individually stable models can generate relatively unstable comparisons, calling into question the validity of CV inference. Specifically, we show that the Lasso and its close cousin, soft-thresholding, generate relatively unstable comparisons and invalid CV inferences, even in the most favorable of learning settings and when both models are individually stable. These findings highlight the importance of verifying relative stability before deploying CV for model comparison.
